"Even for one," etc. This is analogous to the opening case, where one may make use of the light because it was not kindled for him. See Tosafos there, and Rashi and Tosafos in Beitzah 25a.

"And there is no distinction," etc. This is analogous to the case of a non-Jew who comes to extinguish a fire, where the Sages say that the non-Jew acts on his own initiative. It must therefore be understood that here the prohibition is because the Jew derives benefit from the melacha itself, and even when the non-Jew acts on his own initiative it is forbidden. Independently of this point, contracting for work performed in a Jew's house is prohibited, as stated in the Yerushalmi cited by Tosafos at the beginning of Shabbos and by other authorities. See Hagahot Mordechai, beginning of Shabbos, siman 24, at length.

"Since the Jew," etc. Meaning that this differs from sending a letter, where the Jew does not derive benefit from the act of transportation itself, but only from the letter reaching its destination.

"Or for the need of an ill person." See Chullin 15b concerning slaughtering, and likewise concerning a person who is ill but not dangerously so in Eruvin. The principal ruling is like the final approach there, as in Chullin concerning food cooked for an ill person. Tosafos in Gittin explain that only for brit milah did the Sages permit increasing the quantity; see there.

"Or for the need of small children." See Ran at the beginning of Yoma, who explains that this is because such food is their ordinary need, unlike Rashba, who sought to prove from there that one may always directly feed children a rabbinic prohibition. See below, siman 343. The phrase "for the need of small children" means what they genuinely need in significant measure. Otherwise there is no such permission, as appears in Eruvin.

"And some prohibit." This follows the distinction stated there, that the leniency applies where the non-Jew does not know the Jew. The first view holds that, regarding a fire, there is no distinction between a fire kindled for 1 and for 100.

"However, if he did," etc. When the Jew sees the non-Jew doing the melacha, he must protest. Even in the non-Jew's own house the Yerushalmi says that if the Jew sees him performing the work he must protest when it is being done without payment. Here there is no distinction between gratuitous work and paid work, as explained above. This is all the more evident because in the extinguishing case, when the Jew does not see the non-Jew, benefit is permitted and he need not tell him not to extinguish, since the non-Jew acts for himself. Here, by contrast, because the Jew benefits from the melacha itself, he must protest. See Hagahot Mordechai there, where this is discussed at length.

"And if he deliberately placed it upon it," etc. Lamps placed on the table with the intention that a non-Jew remove them the following day have the same law as something forgotten there, so the table does not become a basis for a forbidden item. [Bach]

[1] [Levush] "And on Yom Tov," etc. On Yom Tov there is a prohibition of melacha; on Yom Kippur the punishment is kareit; and on Shabbos the punishment is stoning. This gradation underlies the increase in the number of aliyot. Mateh Moshe gives an allusion: the relevant words contain letter-counts of 3, 5, 4, 6, and 7, and together they equal 25, corresponding to the verse, "Thus shall you bless."

[2] [Levush] "And on Shabbos," etc. The number of aliyot fixed by the Sages corresponds to the sanctity of the day, with 7 on Shabbos, 6 on Yom Kippur, and 5 on Yom Tov. Although additional aliyot may be added on Shabbos, the fixed minimum should not be reduced. The authorities discuss whether additions should be made freely on Yom Tov as well, and the practical custom follows the established communal order.

Where there is a need connected with the honor of Torah, a groom, a brit milah, or other recognized communal obligations, the laws of adding readers are governed by the distinctions stated in siman 282. One should not multiply aliyot in a way that causes unnecessary burdens upon the congregation or disrupts the fixed reading.

In Shulchan Aruch, seif 5, "or his teeth fell out." Mateh Yehudah writes that if he had tooth pain he should not fast, as the later authorities wrote regarding one who merely had thoughts of such a dream. See Chinuch Beit Yehudah, siman 3, and Devar Moshe, siman 22.

[2] [Levush] "Even though we drank," etc. Abudarham explains: "I come to pray, and I ask of You a favorable time for universal atonement." Kol Bo, however, writes: "I hasten to pray to You at the fixed time of Minchah, which is a favorable time." According to Kol Bo, "a favorable time" is not a request; rather, Minchah itself is called a favorable time because Eliyahu was answered then. According to Abudarham there is an additional reason. Since one who is intoxicated may not pray, we ask that this prayer be accepted as a favorable time.

Tanya gives another reason for saying, "As for me, may my prayer to You be at a favorable time," at Shabbos Minchah. The final tribulation, unlike the earlier exiles, will last 9 months. Its final day will be Shabbos, and the distress will intensify beyond all that preceded it until Minchah, when Israel will be answered and the redeemer will come.

In Magen Avraham, seif katan 4, on the words "because," etc. This requires study, because above a different reason was given, namely that pouring first would constitute a defect and a degradation of the mitzvah. Perhaps the text should read, "and also because of an interruption." Although above it appears that the pouring itself does not create a concern of interruption, it is possible that pouring together with extinguishing the lamp constitutes a slight interruption. It appears more likely, however, that there is a scribal error here and that the text should read, "as stated above in the name of Bach," referring to the words of Sefer Chasidim cited above in seif katan 2, which Taz also cites.

"And there is one who disagrees." This refers to the dispute whether women are obligated in Havdalah. The view that exempts them treats Havdalah as a time-bound positive mitzvah that is not inseparably connected with the mitzvah of Shabbos observance. The view that obligates them compares Havdalah to Kiddush, for whoever is included in "Shamor" is included in "Zachor," and women are therefore obligated in the sanctification that marks both the entrance and departure of Shabbos.

According to the stringent opinion, a woman should hear Havdalah from a man who is obligated. Where that is not possible, the authorities discuss whether she may recite Havdalah herself. Since women customarily recite blessings over time-bound positive mitzvot, there is a substantial basis for permitting her to recite it. Nevertheless, where a man can discharge her obligation, that course is preferable.

If one relieves himself in an open place that has no partitions, he should position himself with his face toward the south and his back toward the north, or the reverse. Facing east or west, however, is forbidden. Urinating is permitted in any direction. [Beit Yosef in the name of Rambam]

[7] [Levush] "But not in order to exercise," etc. This means for medicinal purposes, as explained below in siman 332 and in Baal Halachot Gedolot at siman 328, seif 42, unlike Taz. Levush implies that even if one merely walks and does not run, if his intention is exercise it is forbidden. Magen Avraham, however, permits any case in which he is not running. Levush's words appear supported by the Tosefta, chapter 7, which says that an animal that ate too much fruit may be walked about. This implies that doing so for a person is forbidden, and Rama also appears to imply this.

[8] "And it is forbidden to pass through," etc. This is so even when it is impossible to go around. Regarding the reason stated, that he may come to squeeze out the garment, one should not object that soaking the garment is itself laundering and should already be forbidden. Tosafos in Shabbos 111 answer that the rule that soaking is laundering applies only where there is dirt on the garment. One may also answer that this rule does not apply where the dirt is not visible. I found, however, that Sefer Yere'im and Piskei Rekanati answer that the discussion concerns leather garments. This requires study; see siman 302, seif 9.

[9] "He may pass through," etc. This applies even if it is possible to take another route. See siman 333, seif 8. According to Rashi, there is no need for the additional restriction suggested by some authorities. It appears that the explanation is as Tosafos write there, that for the sake of a mitzvah the Sages did not impose the decree concerning squeezing. Sefer HaTerumah and Semak write likewise. See also Rashi at the beginning of Yoma.

The language of Rambam in chapter 19 of Hilchot Shabbos, derived from the Gemara in chapter 6 of Shabbos. Shabbos 15. Explanation: like an iron sickle 1.5 amot long, with an elongated knob at its end. Shabbos 60 and 61. There, 141. There, 60. There, 68, and in accordance with Chiya bar Rav; Rif, Rosh, and Rambam, chapter 19.

[32] [Levush] "It is a burden," etc. Beit Yosef writes this in the name of Rashi and Rabbeinu Yeruham. Malbushei Yom Tov expresses surprise that he did not cite Tosafos, who disagree with Rashi on the basis of an explicit Gemara in Yoma, where the reason is that the item may slip off and he may come to carry it 4 amot in a public domain. If so, the prohibition is only rabbinic. I would add that Ran there, Kol Bo, Hagahot Ashiri, Responsa Rashba, siman 607, and Semag write similarly. Semag explains that because it is made of wood and straw it cannot be tightened securely around the foot, and it may fall off and the wearer may come to carry it.

This makes Beit Yosef's statement that Semag follows Rashi especially difficult. It also appears that Rashi may have given his explanation only according to the initial understanding of the Gemara, whereas according to the conclusion he agrees with the other explanation. Alternatively, Rashi may mean only that it is not considered an ornament because it cannot be fastened in the normal manner of an ornament.

[Levush] "However, if the stump," etc. The Shulchan Aruch omitted this ruling. It appears to be included in what he wrote in seif 16 regarding a pantish, as is implied by Rashba's responsum there.
Rambam, end of chapter 19. Maggid Mishneh writes likewise and states that it is from Tosefta, chapter 8.
There, 146. There, in accordance with R' Eliezer and R' Shimon in the baraita; Rif and Rosh; Rambam, chapter 22; and the other authorities. Rashba in a responsum.

Magen Avraham, seif katan 27: "that it should be like an ornament." This is difficult, for he himself writes in seif katan 14 that carrying it in her hand creates liability even for a woman when it is not perforated, although it is her ornament. If so, why did Magen Avraham here seek only a rabbinic prohibition? There should be actual liability. There is no difficulty. An ornament designed to be worn is not considered an ornament at all when it is carried in the hand. A cane is different, because its normal manner as an ornament is precisely to be carried in the hand.
